title: Judas Defeats Nicanor
sum: Judas gathers six thousand men who have held on to Judaism, and they pray for the ruined city and the blood crying out to God. Now that the Lord's anger has turned to mercy, Judas cannot be stopped (8:1–7). Philip asks for help, and Ptolemy sends Nicanor with twenty thousand men and the general Gorgias. Nicanor plans to pay the king's debt to Rome by selling Jews as slaves, and invites the slave-dealers in advance (8:8–11).

Some of Judas's men desert. The rest pray, and Judas encourages them with the rescues of the past, divides the army among his brothers, reads from the holy book and gives the watchword "God's help" (8:12–23). They kill over nine thousand, but break off the pursuit because the Sabbath is coming. After the Sabbath they share the spoils with the tortured, the widows and the orphans (8:24–29). Timothy and Bacchides are beaten, Callisthenes is burned for burning the Temple gates, and Nicanor flees to Antioch like a runaway slave, admitting that the Jews have a Champion (8:30–36).
readings: Read as the turn from wrath to mercy
The martyrs have died (6–7), and "the Lord's anger had now turned to mercy" (8:5). From this chapter on, the book shows God fighting for a people who keep his law.

The same campaign is told in 1 Maccabees 3:38–4:25 with different leaders, numbers and details. Each book shapes the battle to its own purpose: 1 Maccabees shows Judas's skill, 2 Maccabees God's help and the keeping of the Sabbath.

views.C: Thomas Aquinas asked whether it is lawful to fight on holy days, and answered that it is, when necessity requires; his authority for this is the decision of Mattathias's men to fight if attacked on the Sabbath (Summa Theologiae II–II q. 40 a. 4, citing 1 Maccabees 2:41). Judas's halt in 8:26 is the other side: a pursuit, not a defense, gives way to the holy day.
views.H: Historians generally prefer 1 Maccabees' account of the battle near Emmaus, with Gorgias's night march and Judas's surprise attack on the camp (1 Maccabees 4:1–25). 2 Maccabees leaves those out, makes Nicanor the leader, and adds the Sabbath and the sharing of spoils. Its numbers, six thousand against twenty thousand with nine thousand killed, are round and probably too high.
views.J: Josephus tells this battle from 1 Maccabees: he gives three thousand enemy dead, and he does not mention the Sabbath halt (Antiquities 12.305–312). 2 Maccabees was not kept in Jewish tradition, and the Talmud's Hanukkah story does not use it.

deep.b:
1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees tell the same campaign of 165 BC, and they differ at almost every point. In 1 Maccabees, Lysias sends three generals, Ptolemy, Nicanor and Gorgias, with forty thousand men and seven thousand horsemen (1 Maccabees 3:38–39). Judas gathers at Mizpah, fasts, reads the law and sends the fearful home (1 Maccabees 3:46–56). Gorgias makes a night march to catch him, but Judas leaves his camp, attacks the main enemy camp at dawn, and wins without a long fight. Three thousand enemy fall (1 Maccabees 4:1–25).

In 2 Maccabees, Philip asks Ptolemy for help, Nicanor commands, and Gorgias is only his second (8:8–9). There is no night march and no attack on an empty camp. Instead the book gives a speech, a reading from the holy book, the watchword "God's help", over nine thousand dead, and the Sabbath halt (8:16–28). Nicanor's slave market, which 1 Maccabees mentions in passing (1 Maccabees 3:41), becomes the center of the story: the slave-dealer flees like a slave.

The writer of 2 Maccabees says he abridged a longer history and cared more for the reader's profit than for exact detail (2:24–32). Historians use 1 Maccabees for the course of the battle, and read 2 Maccabees for what the story meant to its readers: a victory that came because the people turned to God and kept his law.

Both books know the problem of the Sabbath in war. Early in the revolt, a thousand Jews in the wilderness let themselves be killed rather than fight on the Sabbath, and Mattathias's men decided to fight back if attacked (1 Maccabees 2:29–41). 2 Maccabees tells of Jews burned in caves while keeping the day (6:11), and it praises the keeping of the Sabbath more than once: here the pursuit stops before the day begins (8:25–28); after another battle the army purifies itself and keeps the Sabbath (12:38); and Nicanor plans to attack on the Sabbath and is destroyed (15:1–5, 28–36).

The book never says that Judas refused to defend himself on the Sabbath. It shows him keeping the day whenever the battle allows. Later Jewish law allowed fighting to save life on the Sabbath, and Christians debated whether the day still binds them at all. That question is asked on the card at Exodus 20.

echoes: Genesis 4:10; Deuteronomy 20:2–8; Deuteronomy 28:10; 2 Kings 19:35; 2 Chronicles 32:7–8; Psalm 20:7; Exodus 20:8–11; 1 Samuel 30:24; Deuteronomy 14:29; 1 Maccabees 3:38–4:25

settings.by: Judas and the six thousand who joined him
settings.when: About 166–165 BC, as the revolt gathered strength in the villages of Judea
settings.why: To ask God to look on his oppressed people, pity the profaned Temple and the ruined city, hear the blood of the murdered and the babies, and show that he hates wickedness.
settings.readers: The prayer is given in reported speech, as the writer summed it up. Where the book's first readers lived is uncertain. The best evidence is the letter set at its front, dated to the year 188 (124 BC) and addressed by the Jews of Jerusalem to the Jews of Egypt, inviting them to keep the new feast (1:1–10); that shows the book, or at least its letters, being sent to Egypt. Whether the abridgment itself was made in Alexandria or in Judea is debated. Within the book, the prayer answers the youngest brother's plea that God's anger stop (7:37–38), and the next verse says it did (8:5).

settings.when: 165 BC, before the battle with Nicanor
settings.why: To keep his men from fear, remind them what the enemy had done to the Temple, the city and the ancestral way of life, and recall the rescues of the past: Sennacherib's army and a battle against the Galatians.
settings.readers: Speeches before battle were a standard part of Greek history writing, and the writer composed this one, as 1 Maccabees composed its own (1 Maccabees 3:58–60; 4:8–11). The Galatian battle in Babylonia (8:20) is known from no other source; it suggests that Jason of Cyrene, whose five books the writer abridged (2:23), drew on stories of Jewish soldiers in Seleucid service that the readers would have heard of.

settings.when: The Sabbath after the battle with Nicanor
settings.why: To bless and praise the Lord who had kept them safe to that day and had begun to show them mercy.
settings.readers: The words are reported, not quoted. 1 Maccabees gives a hymn at this point instead, "For his loyal love is good forever" (1 Maccabees 4:24), sung on the way back from plunder. This book sets the praise on the Sabbath, and it returns to the day in its own scenes: the Jews burned in caves while keeping it (6:11), the army keeping it after another battle (12:38), and Nicanor's plan to attack on it (15:1–5). Its readers were people for whom keeping the Sabbath was a test of loyalty to the law, and the halt here answers the martyrs of 6:11.

settings.when: After the Sabbath, once the spoils had been shared
settings.why: To ask the Lord to be fully reconciled with his servants.
settings.readers: The prayer takes up the book's teaching that God disciplines his people for a short time and then is reconciled with them (5:20; 7:33). It was written for readers who believed that the persecution had been punishment for the people's sin (6:12–16), and who could see the victories that followed as signs that the anger had passed.

settings.to: Those in Antioch and wherever he went
settings.when: After his flight from Judea in 165 BC
settings.why: To explain his defeat: the Jews have a Champion and cannot be wounded while they keep the laws he gave them.
settings.readers: The words are the writer's summary of what Nicanor "went about announcing". Like Heliodorus (3:35–39) and Antiochus (9:12–17), the enemy is made to confess the Jews' God. The book was written for readers who knew that the Temple had been handed over to foreign gods (6:1–5); the confession tells them that the God of the Temple had not been beaten, and that his help depended on keeping the laws.

title: The Death of Antiochus
sum: Antiochus is driven out of Persepolis in disgrace while trying to rob its temples. Near Ecbatana he hears of Nicanor's and Timothy's defeats, and in his fury he orders his driver on to Jerusalem, boasting that he will make the city a graveyard of Jews. God strikes him at once with a pain in his bowels; he is thrown from his chariot, worms swarm in his body, and his flesh rots until no one can bear the smell (9:1–10).

Broken at last, he says that mortals must not think themselves equal to God. He vows to free Jerusalem, make the Jews equal to the Athenians, adorn the Temple, pay for its sacrifices and even become a Jew, but the Lord no longer has mercy on him (9:11–17). Despairing, he writes a courteous letter to the Jews, asking them to keep their goodwill toward his son (9:18–27). He dies in agony in the mountains of a foreign land, and Philip takes the body and flees to Egypt (9:28–29).
readings: Read as judgment that fits the crime

The king who tortured others' bowels is struck in his own (9:5–6), and the man who thought he could touch the stars cannot be carried for his stench (9:10). The chapter is a study in pride brought down.
Read as a warning about late repentance
Antiochus says the right words, "It is right to submit to God", and makes generous vows, but the writer says the Lord "was no longer going to have mercy on him" (9:13).

views.C: Catholic teaching holds that Scripture teaches without error the truth God wished to put into it for our salvation, and that readers must weigh the literary forms and the ways of telling history that writers used in their own time (Dei Verbum 11–12; Divino Afflante Spiritu). The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1910 argued that 9 and 1 Maccabees 6 fit together, and that the letter of 1:13–16 reports a rumor the writer quoted, not one he vouched for.
views.P: Luther kept 2 Maccabees in his Bible's Apocrypha, but in his preface he gave this chapter as one reason against it: the book "describes the death of Antiochus quite differently than does First Maccabees" (Preface to 2 Maccabees, 1534). Protestant readers have treated the story as an edifying example of judgment, not as Scripture.
views.H: Antiochus IV died late in 164 BC in the east; a Babylonian king list records the news in Kislev of the year 148. Polybius says he died mad at Tabae in Persis after failing to rob a temple of Artemis in Elymais (Histories 31.9). This chapter, 1 Maccabees 6 and the letter of 1:13–16 each tell it differently, and the worms and the vow are told in the style of stories about the deaths of tyrants.
views.J: Josephus tells the death from 1 Maccabees: the king falls sick from grief and admits that he suffers for robbing the Temple in Jerusalem, and Josephus rejects Polybius's view that he was punished for the temple in Elymais (Antiquities 12.354–359). On late repentance, the Mishnah says that one who says "I will sin and repent" is not given the chance to repent (Yoma 8:9).

deep.h: One death, told two ways in one book
deep.b:
2 Maccabees gives two accounts of how Antiochus died. In the letter at the front of the book, the priests of the goddess Nanea in Persia kill "Antiochus" and his men in her temple, stoning them through a hidden door in the ceiling, and throw their heads out (1:13–16). In this chapter, God strikes him with an illness on the road, and he dies slowly in the mountains (9:5–28). 1 Maccabees gives a third account (1 Maccabees 6:1–16), and Polybius a fourth. The study on 1 Maccabees 6 compares all of them; the question here is how one book can hold two.

Readers have answered in several ways. (1) The letter is a quoted document. The book does not tell 1:13–16 in its own voice: it quotes a letter from the Jews of Jerusalem to those in Egypt (1:10). On this view the writer, or whoever put the letters in front of the book, passed on what the letter said, and the narrator's own account is the one in this chapter. The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1910 took this line. (2) The letter tells of another king. Some scholars think the story of 1:13–16 fits Antiochus III, who was killed in 187 BC while robbing a temple in Elymais, better than his son. (3) The book was put together from sources. The letters at the front (1:1–2:18) came from elsewhere and were not fitted to the epitome that follows. (4) Both accounts tell a moral truth. Whatever the details, both make the same point: the man who robbed temples died at a temple's door or under God's hand, far from home.

Each answer affects how the book is read as Scripture. Those who hold it inspired point to the quoted letter, or to the writer's purpose. Luther named this chapter as one reason the book should not be counted with the first (Preface to 2 Maccabees). Whether the book is inspired at all is the card on the book's opening page, "Is 2 Maccabees inspired Scripture?"; whether the writer's own admission of weakness (15:38) rules that out is the card beside it.

The king's turn in 9:11–17 sounds like repentance. He comes "to knowledge" under God's whip (9:11), confesses that a mortal must submit to God (9:12), and vows to undo all he has done (9:13–17). But the writer tells the reader at once that the Lord "was no longer going to have mercy on him" (9:13), and the pains do not ease (9:18). The letter that follows asks for loyalty to his son and says nothing of repentance (9:19–27).

The scene raises a question that Christians answer differently: is sorrow that comes from fear of punishment true repentance, and can it come too late? The card below sets out the answers. Two nearby questions are carded elsewhere: whether a penalty remains after God forgives, on the 2 Samuel 12 card ("David was forgiven, yet his child died"), and whether sins must be confessed to a priest, on the Psalm 32 card.

echoes: 2 Chronicles 21:18–19; Isaiah 14:12–15; Isaiah 40:12; Daniel 8:10; Daniel 11:36–45; 2 Kings 5:15–17; Daniel 4:34–37; Acts 12:23; Judith 16:17; 1 Maccabees 6:1–16

settings.to: His charioteer and those around him
settings.when: 164 BC, on the road near Ecbatana after his defeat in Persia
settings.why: To swear revenge on the Jews for the shame of his retreat: he will make Jerusalem a common grave.
settings.readers: The boast is the writer's, placed so that judgment strikes as the words leave the king's mouth (9:5). The book expects its readers to know the stories of proud kings brought down in the prophets: it twice recalls Sennacherib's army destroyed outside Jerusalem (8:19; 15:22), and the king's pride here is told in words close to Isaiah's taunt of the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:13–15).

settings.when: As his illness grew worse, shortly before his death
settings.why: To admit that it is right to submit to God, and that a mortal must not think arrogant thoughts.
settings.readers: The words echo a common Greek saying that mortals must think mortal thoughts, and readers educated in Greek would hear in it the fall of a king whose coins called him "God Manifest". 1 Maccabees gives him a different deathbed speech, addressed to his Friends (1 Maccabees 6:10–13).

settings.when: On his deathbed, in 164 BC
settings.why: To win healing by promising to free Jerusalem, make the Jews equal to the Athenians, restore the Temple vessels, pay for the sacrifices, and become a Jew.
settings.readers: The vow appears only in this book. It was written for Jewish readers who knew that none of it had happened: the Seleucids went on fighting the Jews (10:10–11:12), and the writer has already said that God would not hear it.
views: Many readers note that he offers gifts for healing and never asks forgiveness; the vow is made out of pain, not love of God.
Historians read the vow as the writer's way of making the persecutor undo, in words, each of his crimes.

settings.what: The king's letter to the Jews
settings.when: On his deathbed, late in 164 BC
settings.why: To announce that he has named his son Antiochus king, and to ask the Jews to keep their goodwill toward the boy.
settings.readers: The letter follows the form of real Seleucid letters, with greetings, a report of the king's health, a precedent from his father, and a request. Several commentators, among them Habicht, think the writer took a genuine royal letter announcing the succession, perhaps sent first to another city, and addressed it to the Jews. Its first readers in the book were Jews who knew the boy king as the enemy of 10:10–11:12 and 13.
views: The form and the lack of any repentance suggest a real document set into the story.
Others think the writer wrote it himself, to show a king still keeping up appearances.

traditions.q: Antiochus turns to God and makes his vow only when the pain becomes unbearable, and the writer says the Lord "was no longer going to have mercy on him" (9:13). Is sorrow out of fear of punishment real repentance, and can repentance come too late? (Whether a penalty remains after forgiveness is asked on the 2 Samuel 12 card, and confession to a priest on the Psalm 32 card.)
views: Fear can begin true repentance but cannot finish it alone. The Council of Trent taught that "attrition", sorrow that comes from the ugliness of sin or "from the fear of hell and of punishment", is a gift of God if it rejects the will to sin and hopes for pardon, and that it disposes the sinner to receive grace in the sacrament (session 14, chapter 4). The Catechism adds that by itself it "cannot obtain the forgiveness of grave sins" (paragraph 1453).

Fear is a real but lower beginning. Gregory the Theologian names three ranks of the saved, the slave, the hired servant and the son: "If you are a slave, be afraid of the whip; if you are a hired servant, look only to receive your hire; if you are more than this, a son, revere Him as a Father" (Oration 40.13, NPNF translation). In the same sermon he warns against putting off baptism until the deathbed (40.11–12). On lateness, the Paschal homily ascribed to John Chrysostom, read at every Pascha, says that the Lord "will accept the last even as the first" (OCA translation).

Terror alone is not repentance. Luther taught that the law's terror of conscience is the first part of repentance, but that where the law works alone, without the promise of the gospel, "man must despair, like Saul and Judas"; true repentance joins that terror to faith in the promise of grace (Smalcald Articles III.3, Triglot Concordia translation).

Fear of punishment alone is "legal repentance". Calvin wrote that Cain, Saul and Judas felt their sin and dreaded God's anger, but that such repentance was "nothing better than a kind of threshold to hell"; evangelical repentance looks up and sees in Christ the cure of its wound (Institutes 3.3.4). The Westminster Confession says that repentance unto life springs from the sense "not only of the danger, but also of the filthiness and odiousness" of sin, and from a grasp of God's mercy in Christ (15.2).

title: The Temple Purified and the Riders from Heaven
sum: With the Lord leading them, Judas and his men recover the Temple and the city. They pull down the pagan altars, purify the Temple, light new fire from stones, and offer the first sacrifices in two years, on the very day the Temple had been profaned, 25 Kislev. They keep eight days with joy like the Feast of Booths, which they had missed while hiding in the mountains, carrying branches and palms, and the nation decrees that the days be kept every year (10:1–8).

Under the boy king Eupator, Lysias takes charge, and Ptolemy Macron, the one official who had treated the Jews fairly, is driven to poison himself (10:9–13). Judas storms the Idumean strongholds and punishes those of Simon's men who took a bribe (10:14–23). When Timothy invades with a great army, the Jews pray in sackcloth, and five splendid riders from heaven appear, shield Judas and blind the enemy. Timothy flees to Gazara, which falls after a siege, and he is killed in a cistern (10:24–38).
readings: The book was sent to Egypt with letters inviting Jews there to keep this feast (1:9, 18). Its story of 25 Kislev is the reason the book was written.
Read as the book's pattern of epiphany
The cleansed Temple is defended from heaven: riders appear for those who pray "facing the altar" (10:26, 29). What happened to Heliodorus at the Temple (3:24–26) now happens on the battlefield.

views.C: The Catechism notes that Jesus went up to the Temple for the feasts, and among the passages it cites is John's account of the Festival of Dedication (Catechism 583; John 10:22–23). Catholic readers find in this chapter the beginning of a feast at which Jesus taught; whether the church may set up holy days of its own is the card on 1 Maccabees 4.
views.P: Many Protestants note that Jesus kept a feast the law of Moses does not command (John 10:22). The Westminster Directory, on the other hand, ruled that festival days "having no warrant in the word of God, are not to be continued", keeping only the Lord's Day; this question too belongs to the card on 1 Maccabees 4.
views.H: The link with the Feast of Booths in 10:6 has led some historians to see Hanukkah as a delayed Booths, kept in Kislev because the autumn feast had been missed. Others think the eight days follow the dedication of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 8:65–66). The heavenly riders are told in the style of Greek temple histories, in which gods appear to defend their shrines; Pausanias tells how the Galatians were driven from Delphi in 279 BC by signs from the god (Description of Greece 10.23).
views.J: Hanukkah is still kept for eight days from 25 Kislev. Josephus calls it "Lights" (Antiquities 12.325); the Talmud tells of one jar of oil that burned for eight days (Shabbat 21b); and the prayer Al ha-Nissim, said at Hanukkah, thanks God for the days of Mattathias and his sons. Jewish tradition kept none of this chapter's details: neither the fire from stones nor the link with Booths.

deep.h: From Booths in Kislev to Hanukkah
deep.b:
Both books of Maccabees date the cleansing to 25 Kislev and set up an eight-day feast (1 Maccabees 4:52–59; 10:5–8). 1 Maccabees calls it "the days of the dedication of the altar". 2 Maccabees explains the eight days in its own way: the people kept them "as one keeps the Feast of Booths", because they had spent the last Booths hiding in mountains and caves (10:6). They carried branches and palms, as at Booths (Leviticus 23:40). The letters at the front of the book invite the Jews of Egypt to keep the feast too (1:9, 18).

Later the feast took other names. John calls it "the Festival of Dedication" (John 10:22). Josephus calls it "Lights" and supposes the name came from the freedom that had dawned on them (Antiquities 12.325). The Talmud asks, "What is Hanukkah?" and answers with a jar of oil sealed by the high priest that burned for eight days (Shabbat 21b). Neither book of Maccabees knows that story; 2 Maccabees has fire struck from stones instead (10:3), and in the letter, holy fire hidden at the exile and found again in Nehemiah's time (1:18–36).

Christians have remembered the feast mostly because Jesus was in the Temple "in Solomon's Porch" at it (John 10:23). Whether a people of God may set up a feast that the law does not command is the card on 1 Maccabees 4.

2 Maccabees calls its story one of "appearances from heaven" (2:21), and the riders of this chapter are the clearest example. A rider in golden armor and two young men strike Heliodorus at the Temple (3:25–26); horsemen are seen in the sky over Jerusalem for forty days (5:2–4); five riders shield Judas and blind the enemy (10:29–30); a rider in white leads the army to Beth-zur (11:8); and before the last battle Judas sees Jeremiah in a dream (15:12–16).

The 66 books know a heavenly army: Elisha's servant sees "horses and fiery chariots" (2 Kings 6:17), and Joshua meets "the commander of the LORD's army" (Joshua 5:14). But only Revelation shows its riders going into battle (Revelation 19:11–14). Catholic and Orthodox readers have read the riders as angels sent by God, as Judas himself prays for "a good angel" (11:6; 15:23). Historians compare the Greek stories in which gods or heroes appear to defend a shrine or a city. Whether each believer has a guardian angel is asked on the card at Tobit 5.

echoes: Leviticus 6:13; Leviticus 9:24; Leviticus 23:34–43; 1 Kings 8:65–66; 2 Chronicles 7:9; 2 Chronicles 29:17; John 10:22–23; John 12:13; Revelation 7:9; Exodus 23:22; 2 Kings 6:17–18; Genesis 19:11; Joshua 5:14; Revelation 19:11–14; Hebrews 11:38

settings.when: December 164 BC, after the first sacrifices on the new altar
settings.why: To ask the Lord never again to let them fall into such evils, and if they sin, to correct them himself, gently, and not hand them over to blasphemous, barbarian nations.
settings.readers: The prayer states the book's teaching on suffering (6:12–16) in the words of the people. Readers who kept the feast every year, as the letter at the front of the book asks the Jews of Egypt to do (1:9), would hear it as a prayer of their own at the feast.

settings.by: The Jewish assembly, by public order and vote
settings.to: The whole nation of the Jews
settings.when: December 164 BC
settings.why: To set up the eight days as a feast to be kept every year.
settings.readers: The decree is given in the language of a Greek city's vote. Its first known readers outside Judea were the Jews of Egypt, to whom the Jews of Jerusalem wrote, in the year 188 (124 BC), urging them to keep the feast (1:1–9). Whether the second letter (1:10–2:18) is as early is debated.

settings.what: A solemn prayer before the attack
settings.when: About 163 BC, before the attack on the Idumean strongholds
settings.why: To ask God to fight as their ally.
settings.readers: The prayer is only mentioned. The writer places prayer before every battle (8:2–4; 10:25–26; 11:6; 12:36; 15:21–24), and readers learn that Judas's victories come from God, not from numbers.

settings.by: Judas's men, lying before the altar
settings.when: About 163 BC, as Timothy's army approached
settings.why: To ask God to be merciful and to be the enemy of their enemies, as the law promises (Exodus 23:22).
settings.readers: The prayer quotes the Greek Exodus, which shows a writer and readers who knew the law in Greek. The setting, "on the platform facing the altar", is the Temple just cleansed, and the answer, the five riders, comes in the battle that follows.

settings.when: After the fall of Gazara
settings.why: To bless the Lord who is the great benefactor of Israel and gives them victory.
settings.readers: "Benefactor" was the title Greek cities gave to kings and patrons, and several Seleucid and Ptolemaic kings were called Euergetēs. The writer uses the word with that weight: he calls the high priest Onias "the man who did good to the city" (4:2, where the Greek is euergetēs). Here the title is given to God, for readers who knew it as a king's honor.

title: Lysias Defeated, and the Four Letters
sum: Lysias, the boy king's guardian, marches with eighty thousand men, the whole cavalry and eighty elephants, meaning to make Jerusalem a Greek city, tax the Temple and sell the high priesthood every year. He besieges Beth-zur. Judas's men pray with tears for a good angel, and as they set out a rider in white with golden armor appears at their head. They charge like lions, and Lysias flees (11:1–12).

Seeing that God fights for the Hebrews, Lysias makes peace and persuades the king (11:13–15). Four letters follow: Lysias to the Jews, promising to put their requests to the king (11:16–21); the young king to Lysias, giving back the Temple and the ancestral laws now that his father has died (11:22–26); a king to the Jewish council, granting an amnesty to those who return home by the end of Xanthicus (11:27–33); and two Roman envoys to the Jews, backing Lysias's concessions (11:34–38).
readings: Read as the end of the persecution
The king's letter says what the whole revolt fought for: the Temple given back and life "by the customs of their ancestors" (11:25).
Read as a file of documents
The writer has set four real-looking letters side by side. Their dates and order do not fit his story, and historians use them to rebuild the order of events.

views.C: The Catholic Encyclopedia of 1910 argued that this campaign of Lysias is not the one of 1 Maccabees 4, so that the two books do not conflict.
views.P: Luther observed that 2 Maccabees "reports several incidents that happened before those reported in the first book", and concluded that it could not really be a second book (Preface to 2 Maccabees, 1534). The order of this chapter is one such case.
views.H: Most historians think the battle of 11:1–12 is Lysias's first campaign, of 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:26–35), set here after the death of Antiochus. The four letters are widely accepted as genuine documents. On the usual reconstruction, the letter to the council (11:27–33) comes from Antiochus IV in spring 164; Lysias's letter (11:16–21) and the Roman letter belong to the same months; and the young king's letter (11:22–26) belongs to the peace of 163 or 162 BC.
views.J: Josephus tells only the peace of 1 Maccabees 6: Lysias advises the young king to grant the Jews their laws, and the king later has Menelaus put to death at Berea (Antiquities 12.379–385). He does not use these letters.

deep.b:
The writer gives four letters without explaining how they fit together. (1) Lysias to the Jews, dated the year 148 in an unknown month, "Dioscorinthius" (11:16–21). (2) King Antiochus to Lysias, undated, saying "Our father has gone over to the gods" and returning the Temple (11:22–26). (3) King Antiochus to the Jewish council, dated 15 Xanthicus 148, granting an amnesty to those who come home by the thirtieth (11:27–33). (4) Two Roman envoys to the Jews, dated the same day (11:34–38).

The year 148 of the Seleucid era ran from autumn 165 to autumn 164 BC in the Macedonian reckoning, so Xanthicus 148 is spring 164, months before the Temple was cleansed and before Antiochus IV died. Letter (2), which speaks of the father's death, must come later, from Antiochus V. So the letters cannot all belong to the story of this chapter, which comes after the king's death.

Many historians, following Habicht and others, put them in this order: Lysias's letter (1) and the Romans' letter (4) in 164, during talks after Lysias's defeat; the king's amnesty (3) from Antiochus IV in spring 164; and the young king's letter (2) at the peace of 163 or 162, when the Temple and the laws were formally given back (1 Maccabees 6:57–61). Others date them differently, and the unknown month makes certainty impossible. The writer seems to have gathered all the documents of the peace in one place, after his story of Lysias's defeat.

echoes: Exodus 23:20; Psalm 34:7; 2 Kings 6:17; Revelation 19:11–14; 1 Maccabees 3:4; Genesis 49:9; Numbers 35:25; 1 Maccabees 4:26–35; 1 Maccabees 6:57–61

settings.when: About 164 BC, when Lysias was besieging Beth-zur
settings.why: To beg the Lord with tears to send a good angel to save Israel.
settings.readers: The prayer looks back to the angel God promised at the Exodus (Exodus 23:20) and forward to Judas's last prayer for a good angel (15:23). Readers who knew Tobit, whose Aramaic and Hebrew copies were found at Qumran, knew the same hope in Tobit's words, "For a good angel will go with him" (Tobit 5:22).

settings.when: On the march, after the rider in white appeared
settings.why: To bless God for the sign, and to take courage.
settings.readers: Only reported. The writer pairs each heavenly sign with praise, as in 8:27 and 10:38.

settings.when: The year 148 of the Seleucid era (165–164 BC), in the unknown month "Dioscorinthius"
settings.why: To report that he has put the Jews' requests, brought by John and Absalom, to the king, and to promise further help if they stay loyal.
settings.readers: The first readers were the Jewish leaders who had sent John and Absalom. The letter names no high priest and does not name Judas, which suggests a community still without an accepted head. Its form matches Hellenistic official letters known from inscriptions, which is one reason historians accept it as genuine.

settings.what: The young king's letter to Lysias
settings.when: After the death of Antiochus IV; probably 163 or 162 BC
settings.why: To end the conflict: the Temple is to be given back and the Jews may live by their ancestral customs; Lysias is to assure them.
settings.readers: The letter was written to Lysias, not to the Jews, and reached them as a copy. It admits that "our father's plan to bring them over to Greek ways" had failed, which made it precious to the Jewish readers who preserved it. Some historians date it to the peace of 1 Maccabees 6:57–61.

settings.what: The king's letter to the Jewish council
settings.to: The council of elders and the rest of the Jews
settings.when: 15 Xanthicus of the year 148, spring 164 BC
settings.why: To offer an amnesty: those who return home by 30 Xanthicus may live by their own food laws and laws, and none will be punished for what they did unknowingly.
settings.readers: The first readers were the council and the Jews loyal to the king, with Menelaus as the go-between. Rebels in the hills were meant to hear it and come home. The deadline of fifteen days suggests that the revolt was still going on, before the Temple was retaken.
views: Most historians, because of the date and the amnesty, assign it to the old king before his death.
Some read the letter as the young king's, as the book's order implies, and explain the date differently.

settings.by: Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, envoys of Rome
settings.when: 15 Xanthicus of the year 148, spring 164 BC
settings.why: To approve Lysias's concessions and invite the Jews to send someone quickly, since the envoys were on their way to Antioch.
settings.readers: If genuine, it is the oldest document of contact between Rome and the Jews, earlier than Judas's treaty of 161 BC (1 Maccabees 8). Its readers would see Rome as a friend, as 1 Maccabees 8 does. Some historians doubt it because the envoys' names are not found elsewhere in that form.
